 • For each friend i, a meeting start time s[i] (in minutes taken from 9:00AM) that must lie within that friend’s available window and allow enough time for the minimum meeting duration.
 • We fix each friend’s meeting duration to its minimum required time (Andrew 75, Sarah 15, Nancy 60, Rebecca 90, Robert 30).

In addition the route (order of visits) must obey travel‐time constraints. In our formulation we assume a candidate ordering – one that our reasoning shows is “good” – namely:
 Order = [Robert, Rebecca, Andrew, Sarah, Nancy]
which in our index–to–friend mapping is:
 Index 4: Robert (The Castro)
 Index 3: Rebecca (Chinatown)
 Index 0: Andrew (Golden Gate Park)
 Index 1: Sarah (Pacific Heights)
 Index 2: Nancy (Presidio)

The constraints are then formulated as follows:
 • For the very first meeting, the meeting start time must be no earlier than the travel time from the start location (Union Square) to that friend’s location.
 • For every meeting, the meeting must “fit” in the friend’s available window. For example, Andrew is available from 11:45AM (165 minutes after 9:00AM) to 2:30PM (330 minutes), so his meeting start must be ≥165 and his meeting must finish by 330.
 • Between meetings, if friend j is visited immediately after friend i then we require:
  s[j] ≥ (s[i] + d[i] + travel_time(i → j))
 For example, after meeting Robert (at The Castro), we must leave and allow 20 extra minutes to go from The Castro to Chinatown (Rebecca’s location).
 • Since some friends are available later than the earliest possible arrival (for example, Sarah is available only from 16:15), the schedule may include “waiting” time.
 • Finally, we can set an objective of minimizing the overall finish time (or equivalently the sum of extra waiting), so that our “optimal” schedule minimizes idle time while ensuring that we meet our goal of meeting as many friends as possible.

 • A meeting finish time finish[f] = start[f] + d[f].

We model your day’s schedule as a constraint satisfaction problem in which we decide:
 • The order in which you meet your five friends (each meeting happens at a distinct location), and
 • The starting time for each meeting.
  
The problem has the following ingredients:
 1. Decision Variables:
  – order[k]: an integer (0…4) representing which friend is scheduled in the kth meeting slot.
  – T[k]: the starting time (in minutes, relative to 9:00AM) at which you start meeting that friend.
  
 2. Constraints:
  – Domain constraints: Each order variable is between 0 and 4 and all are different (permutation).
  – Meeting availability: For any friend i meeting in position k, T[k] must be no earlier than the friend’s availability start time and T[k] + minimum meeting duration must be no later than the friend’s availability end time.
  – Travel requirements: You start at the Presidio at 9:00AM. For the first meeting, your meeting time cannot start before you have traveled from the Presidio to that friend’s location. For each subsequent meeting, T[k] must be at least the end time of the previous meeting plus the travel time from the previous meeting’s location to the current friend’s location.
   • Note: Be cautious when looking up travel times because the travel time from a location to itself isn’t given. Although our ordering ensures friends are distinct, we must “guard” against the lookup when i and j are equal.
  
 3. (Optional) Objective:
  – We can minimize the time when your day finishes (the end time of the last meeting), effectively “packing” the schedule.

Step 1 – Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem:
---------------------------------------------------------
We can view this “friend‐meeting” itinerary as a scheduling problem with temporal and spatial constraints. In our formulation the “variables” are the meeting‐start times (in minutes from midnight) for each friend visit. For each friend we have:

• A location (e.g. Golden Gate Park for Jeffrey, The Castro for Deborah, etc.) with a fixed “available window” (start and end times) and a minimum meeting duration.
• A travel segment from the previous location to the friend’s location. For example, you begin at Nob Hill (arrival fixed at 9:00AM) and then travel to Golden Gate Park in 17 minutes. In general, the arrival time at a friend’s location is “previous meeting’s finish time + travel time”.
• A waiting decision if you arrive before your friend’s available slot begins. In our model this is “absorbed” by requiring the meeting start time to be no less than both the arrival time at the location and the friend’s available start time.
• The meeting’s finish time equals “meeting start time + required duration”. This must be no later than the friend’s available end time.

We then add constraints for every friend:
 – For example, for Jeffrey (at Golden Gate Park): if you arrive at Nob Hill at 9:00 (which is 9×60 = 540 minutes), you reach Golden Gate Park at 540+17 = 557 minutes. Since Jeffrey is available only starting at 11:15AM (675 minutes), you have to wait until then. Moreover, you must spend at least 120 minutes with him and finish by 2:30PM (870 minutes).
 – Similar constraints are set for Deborah, Margaret, Ronald, and Emily with travel times (as given in the problem) inserted between the meetings.
Finally, one can use an objective function (for instance, minimizing the finishing time of the last meeting) to “optimize” the schedule. In our case the schedule that meets all friends while minimizing idle time is chosen.

We model the “day‐in‐SF” scheduling problem as a constraint satisfaction problem. You start at Presidio at 9:00AM and wish to “meet” each friend at their designated location during their available window – but only if you can also remain long enough to satisfy the minimum meeting duration. In addition, you must “travel” between locations; each travel segment takes a fixed number of minutes that depends on the pair of locations.

Our decision variables are:
 • For each friend i (Jessica, Ashley, Ronald, William, Daniel):
  – S[i]: the meeting’s start time (in minutes from midnight)
  – E[i]: the meeting’s end time (in minutes from midnight)
 • For each friend i a schedule order integer order[i] (with values 0–4) to determine in which sequence you visit the friends. The friend with order 0 is visited first (coming directly from Presidio) and for any two friends i and j that are visited consecutively – that is, if order[i]+1 = order[j] – the constraint requires that the start of j’s meeting occurs no earlier than the completion of i’s meeting plus the travel time from friend i’s location to friend j’s location.

In addition, we impose these constraints:
 • Each meeting i must occur fully within that friend’s “availability window.” For example, Jessica is at Golden Gate Park between 1:45PM (825 minutes) and 3:00PM (900 minutes).
 • The meeting duration E[i] – S[i] must be at least the given minimum.
 • If a friend is scheduled first (order 0), the meeting’s S[i] must be no earlier than your departure time from Presidio (9:00AM, i.e. 540 minutes) plus the travel time from Presidio to that friend’s location.
 • The “consecutive‐visit” constraint is imposed by checking for any two friends i and j that satisfy order[i]+1 = order[j]: in that case S[j] must be at least E[i] plus the travel time from friend i’s location to friend j’s location.

Our overall goal is to “meet as many friends as possible” – i.e. find a schedule that includes all meetings while satisfying the above time–window and travel–time constraints. (In our model all 5 meetings are made; an objective function could be added if one wished to choose a schedule with minimal waiting time.)

    # Friend names and corresponding meeting locations.
    friend_names = ["Rebecca", "Amanda", "James", "Sarah", "Melissa"]
    friend_locations = ["Bayview", "Pacific Heights", "Alamo Square", "Fisherman's Wharf", "Golden Gate Park"]

    # James: 9:45AM to 9:15PM, Sarah: 8:00AM to 9:30PM, Melissa: 9:00AM to 6:45PM.
    avail_start = [540, 1110, 585, 480, 540]  # 9:00AM, 6:30PM, 9:45AM, 8:00AM, 9:00AM
    avail_end   = [765, 1305, 1275, 1290, 1125]  # 12:45PM, 9:45PM, 9:15PM, 9:30PM, 6:45PM
    meeting_duration = 90

    # Travel times from The Castro to a friend’s location.
    # (The Castro to Bayview, Pacific Heights, Alamo Square, Fisherman's Wharf, Golden Gate Park)
    travel_from_castro = [19, 16, 8, 24, 11]

    # Travel time matrix between friend locations.
    # Order of friend locations: [Bayview, Pacific Heights, Alamo Square, Fisherman's Wharf, Golden Gate Park]
    travel_matrix = [
        [0,   23, 16, 25, 22],  # from Bayview
        [22,   0, 10, 13, 15],  # from Pacific Heights
        [16,  10,  0, 19, 9],   # from Alamo Square
        [26,  26, 12,  0, 25],  # from Fisherman's Wharf
        [23,  16, 10, 24, 0]    # from Golden Gate Park
    ]
    
    num_friends = 5

    # --- Create Z3 optimization object ---
    opt = Optimize()

    # Decision variables:
    # "order" represents the sequence in which to visit the friends (a permutation of 0..4)
    order = [Int("order_%d" % i) for i in range(num_friends)]
    # "m" represents the meeting start times (in minutes from midnight) for the scheduled meeting in that order slot.
    m = [Int("m_%d" % i) for i in range(num_friends)]

    # Add constraints that each order variable is between 0 and 4 and all orders are distinct.
    for i in range(num_friends):
        opt.add(order[i] >= 0, order[i] < num_friends)
    opt.add(Distinct(order))

    # Meeting window constraints.
    # For the meeting scheduled in slot i, if order[i]==a then the meeting must start between avail_start[a] 
    # and avail_end[a]-meeting_duration (so that a full 90-minute meeting fits).
    for i in range(num_friends):
        lower_bound_expr = Sum([If(order[i] == a, avail_start[a], 0) for a in range(num_friends)])
        upper_bound_expr = Sum([If(order[i] == a, avail_end[a] - meeting_duration, 0) for a in range(num_friends)])

—————— REASONING ——————
We can view the day’s itinerary as a constraint–satisfaction (and optimization) problem. We must “schedule” meetings with a set of friends – each meeting has these parameters:
 • A friend f is “available” only during a given time‐window [avail_start,avail_end] (expressed in minutes after midnight) and requires a minimum meeting duration.
 • You start at a fixed location (Fisherman’s Wharf at 9:00AM, i.e. minute 540) and then travel among locations. We are given the travel times between every pair of locations.
 • For any friend f that you choose to meet, you must arrive “in time” – that is, the meeting’s start must be no earlier than the maximum of the friend’s available‐start and the earliest time you could arrive from Fisherman’s Wharf (i.e. 540 + travel_time(Fisherman’s Wharf,f_loc)).
 • If you schedule two meetings f and g (in whichever order) then one must come entirely before the other – meaning that if f is scheduled before g then the end time for f plus the travel time from f’s location to g’s location (a fixed number) must be less than or equal to the start time for g. (Since meetings cannot overlap and you cannot be in two places at once, the transitions must “fit”.)

1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have nine friends located in various San Francisco neighborhoods. Each friend is available during a given time‐window and you need to “meet” them for at least a prescribed minimum amount of minutes. You start your day at 9:00AM in the Marina District.  • If you do, what “meeting start time” (and hence meeting end time = start time + minimum required meeting duration) you plan.

 – For each friend i, an integer “start” time (in minutes after 9:00AM) and an “end” time defined by start + minimum meeting duration.
 – For each friend i, an “order” integer that tells us the position in the day’s itinerary.

2. It adds constraints so that if you choose to meet a friend the meeting must happen during the friend’s available window (and can’t start before you could possibly get there from Mission District).
3. For every pair of attended meetings, it forces one to occur (with its travel time) before the other.
4. The objective is to maximize the total count of meetings. (Due to conflicting availability windows, you might not be able to schedule all nine.)
5. After the model is found, the code “simulates” your day by ordering the meetings by their start time, “computing” travel from your starting location to each friend and then waiting if needed.

Step\xa01. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have nine friends each with a fixed location, an availability window (start and end times expressed in minutes from midnight) and a minimum meeting duration. You start at Mission District at 9:00AM (540 minutes). In planning your day you must decide (a) which friends to “visit” (our decision booleans) and (b) at what minute (an integer variable) you begin meeting each friend. In addition, between every pair of meetings (for friends you decide to visit) you must “travel” from one friend’s district to the next. The travel times (which are not necessarily symmetric) are given.

For every friend i that you meet, if you decide to “attend” (visit) the meeting then the meeting’s start time must be at least:
 • the friend’s own available‐start time,
 • the time needed to travel from Mission District (your starting point) to that friend’s district.
Also the meeting must finish before the friend’s available–end time (that is, start time plus the fixed minimum duration fits in the window).

Furthermore, if you decide to meet two different friends i and j then one meeting must completely finish (including the subsequent travel from i’s district to j’s district) before the other meeting starts. In other words, for each pair of friends i,j (with i ≠ j) that you choose to attend, you add the disjunctive “no–overlap” constraint: either

 start_i + duration_i + (travel time from friend i to friend j) ≤ start_j  
or  
 start_j + duration_j + (travel time from friend j to friend i) ≤ start_i.

Because some of the friends’ time windows severely conflict with others (for example, Mary is available only from 4:45–6:45PM with a 120‐minute meeting and Deborah is only available from 7:00–8:45PM with a 105‐minute meeting while Karen’s window from 6:00–8:15PM would conflict with one or both), not all nine meetings can be scheduled. Our goal (the optimization objective) is to “attend” as many meetings as possible, that is, to maximize the sum of the visit–booleans.

Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have nine friends each with a fixed location, an availability window (start and end times expressed in minutes from midnight) and a minimum meeting duration. You start at Mission District at 9:00AM (540 minutes). In planning your day you must decide (a) which friends to “visit” (our decision booleans) and (b) at what minute (an integer variable) you begin meeting each friend. In addition, between every pair of meetings (for friends you decide to visit) you must “travel” from one friend’s district to the next. The travel times (which are not necessarily symmetric) are given.

For every friend i that you meet, if you decide to “attend” (visit) the meeting then the meeting’s start time must be at least:
 • the friend’s own available‐start time,
 • the time needed to travel from Mission District (your starting point) to that friend’s district.
Also the meeting must finish before the friend’s available–end time (that is, start time plus the fixed minimum duration fits in the window).

Furthermore, if you decide to meet two different friends i and j then one meeting must completely finish (including the subsequent travel from i’s district to j’s district) before the other meeting starts. In other words, for each pair of friends i,j (with i ≠ j) that you choose to attend, you add the disjunctive “no–overlap” constraint: either

 start_i + duration_i + (travel time from friend i to friend j) ≤ start_j  
or  
 start_j + duration_j + (travel time from friend j to friend i) ≤ start_i.

Our goal (the optimization objective) is to “attend” as many meetings as possible, that is, to maximize the sum of the visit–booleans.

Explanation:

• The script defines variables s_i (start times) and v_i (whether to meet friend i) for each friend.
• It adds constraints ensuring that if a friend is scheduled:
 – The meeting starts no earlier than the friend’s availability and finishes by their end time.
 – The meeting cannot begin before you arrive (after traveling from Richmond).
• For every pair of scheduled meetings (i,j) a disjunctive “ordering” constraint is imposed so that the earlier meeting—in addition to its duration plus necessary travel time—finishes before the next meeting starts.
• The objective is to maximize the sum of v_i – the number of friends met.
• Once solved, the script sorts the scheduled meetings in chronological order and “simulates” the day by computing travel and waiting times. Finally it prints a list of strings in the style of:
  ["You start at Richmond District at 9:00AM.", "You travel to Financial District in 22 minutes and arrive at 9:22AM.", …]

Between any pair of “meeting locations” there is a fixed “travel time” (for example, 8 minutes from The Castro to Alamo Square and various travel times between other neighborhoods).

The “decision variables” are:
  • For each friend i, a Boolean variable meet[i] that indicates whether we schedule a meeting.
  • For each friend i, an integer variable start[i] that gives the meeting’s start time (in minutes from midnight).

Each meeting must obey the constraints:
  – If you meet friend i then your meeting must start no earlier than his availability start and finish (start[i] + duration) no later than his availability end.
  – Moreover, even if friend i is not the very first on the day, the time at which you can “arrive” at i’s location is bounded by the travel time from “The Castro” (your start location) – that is, start[i] ≥ 9:00AM + travel_time(The Castro, friend_i’s location).

A key “no‐overlap” constraint is that if you meet two different friends i and j then either i’s meeting (plus the travel time from i to j) must finish before j’s meeting starts, or vice‐versa:
  If both meet[i] and meet[j] then
    start[i] + duration_i + travel_time(location_i,location_j) ≤ start[j]
   or
    start[j] + duration_j + travel_time(location_j,location_i) ≤ start[i].

Finally, the objective is to “maximize the number of friends met” (i.e. maximize the sum of the meet[i] indicator variables). One then “searches” for integer start times that “line up” a feasible itinerary meeting all the window, duration and travel‐time constraints.

1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have a “day‐planner problem” where you start at a fixed location (“The Castro” at 9:00AM) and want to “visit” a set of friends – each at a different neighborhood – satisfying two kinds of constraints:
  • Time–window constraints. For each friend the meeting may only occur during the friend’s available interval and you must “meet” for at least a given duration. (For example, Elizabeth is at Marina District from 7:00PM to 8:45PM and you must spend at least 105 minutes with her. In effect you can only “meet” her if you schedule an interval [s, s+105] ⊆ [7:00PM, 8:45PM].)
  • Travel time constraints. To “move” from one friend’s location to the next you incur a travel time – these are given (and note the matrix is not perfectly symmetric). In addition the first meeting must be reachable from “The Castro” by 9:00AM plus travel time.
  
We also have a “goal:” to meet as many friends as possible. (Some friends – like Ronald, for example – have windows that are impossible to satisfy given the start time and travel times; the model should choose not to “attend” those meetings.)

To model the problem we introduce, for each friend i the following decision variables:
  • x[i] ∈ {true, false} – a Boolean that indicates if you schedule his/her visit.
  • s[i] ∈ ℤ – the meeting “start time” (in minutes after midnight) when you begin meeting friend i.
  • pos[i] ∈ ℤ – the “position” or order in the visited schedule (if x[i] is true, pos[i] ≥ 1; if x[i] is false, we set pos[i] = 0).

For each friend i (with data: available interval [a_i, b_i] and minimum meeting duration d_i) we require that if x[i] is true then:
  • s[i] ≥ max(a_i, 540 + travel_time("The Castro", location_i)) if friend i is the first meeting (i.e. if pos[i] = 1)
  • s[i] + d_i ≤ b_i

For any two friends i and j that are both “attended” (x[i] and x[j] true) we enforce that they are not scheduled simultaneously. In our encoding we require that their ordering (given by pos[i] and pos[j]) is different and that the times “fit in sequence”. That is, if friend i comes before friend j (pos[i] < pos[j]) then the meeting with friend i must be finished and enough time allowed to travel to friend j’s location:
  
  s[i] + d_i + travel_time(location_i, location_j) ≤ s[j].

Finally, the objective is to maximize the number of friends visited, i.e. maximize Σᵢ [if x[i] then 1 else 0]. (We use the minimum meeting durations exactly so that any extra time “waiting” is saved for additional meetings.)

In effect you can only “meet” her if you schedule an interval [s, s+105] ⊆ [7:00PM, 8:45PM].)
  • Travel time constraints. To “move” from one friend’s location to the next you incur a travel time – these are given (and note the matrix is not perfectly symmetric). In addition the first meeting must be reachable from “The Castro” by 9:00AM plus travel time.
  
We also have a “goal:” to meet as many friends as possible. (Some friends – like Ronald, for example – have windows that are impossible to satisfy given the start time and travel times; the model should choose not to “attend” those meetings.)

  • pos[i] ∈ ℤ – the “position” or order in the visited schedule (if x[i] is true, pos[i] ≥ 1; if x[i] is false, we set pos[i] = 0).
